title: Sherpa Tensing — Descent Four: Present Perfect Passive (B1)
description: The tense of announcements. Something happened, it is finished, and it matters now — and the passive lets you say so without naming whoever did it. The…

hero.lede: The tense of announcements. Something happened, it is finished, and it matters now — and the passive lets you say so without naming whoever did it. The decision has been taken. By whom? The sentence declines to say.

sections.label: Descent briefing
sections.title: When to use it
sections.lead: The passive is not a different tense. It is the present perfect with the doer let go — and the reason you let them go is always one of these six.

cards.head: You do not know who
cards.body: Nobody can tell you the doer, so the sentence does without one.

cards.head: The doer does not matter
cards.body: The event is the news; who did it is a footnote.

cards.head: The doer is obvious
cards.body: Saying it would be a waste of everyone's time.

cards.head: You would rather not say
cards.body: The passive is how English removes a person from a sentence.

cards.head: Putting the important thing first
cards.body: Whatever you put at the front is what the sentence is about.

cards.head: Putting the doer back with by
cards.body: When the doer is the point, it goes at the end.
cards.ex: "The report has been signed off by the board."

cards.head: Negative
cards.body: the not goes after the first auxiliary

cards.head: Questions
cards.body: the first auxiliary moves to the front

charts.head: Turning an active sentence around
charts.note: Three moves, always the same: the object comes to the front, the verb becomes has / have + been + participle, and the old subject either disappears or goes to the back behind by. Only the middle step changes from camp to camp.

head: Active
Passive
What moved
rows: The board has signed off the report.
The report has been signed off by the board.
The board stayed, at the end.
They have flooded three hundred homes.
Three hundred homes have been flooded.

charts.head: Conjugation chart
charts.note: Been is fixed and the participle is fixed. Only has or have changes — and note that been and the participle are two different words doing two different jobs.

charts.head: Three mistakes worth naming
charts.note: Almost every error with this one is one of these three.

head: Not this
This
Why
rows: After been comes the third form. Stole is the second.
Without been the bike is the thief.
Happen takes no object, so it has no passive.

charts.note: Neither is better. The question is only what the sentence is about — because whatever you put at the front is what the reader will think it is about.

head: Question
Passive
Active
rows:
The thing it happens to.
"My bike has been stolen."

The one who does it.
"Someone has stolen my bike."
Often not — and you do not need to.
Yes, and you are naming them.
At the end with by, or nowhere at all.
At the front, as the subject.
Longer by two or three words.
Usually shorter. Prefer it when both work.

charts.example: This is the sentence a company writes when something has gone wrong: an error has been identified, your account has been suspended, the changes have been made. Finished, relevant now, and nobody at the wheel. Being able to hear the missing subject is half the value of learning it.

sections.label: Trail markers
sections.title: Signal words

signals.head: Verbs with no passive at all

sections.example: The test for whether a verb can go passive: does it take an object? They built it has one, so it turns. It happened has none, so it cannot.

sections.label: Interactive
sections.title: The event, and the doer you dropped

diagram.intro: The block is the same block as the ascent, lit from above instead of fading into the dark — because the tense has not changed, only the light. Inside it sits a dashed box: the doer. It is drawn inside the event rather than beside it because the doer is not a moment in time, it is a part of the sentence — and it is dashed because most of the time nobody says it. Click either to see it in a sentence.

panels.head: The doer — optional, and usually gone
items: … and the river gets no mention either.

quiz.explain: Has + been + the third form. Steal / stole / stolen.

quiz.hint: Since points at the present perfect.
quiz.explain: Since needs a perfect, and the bridge is not doing the closing.
Homes is plural, so have been, and the participle flooded.
Hasn't + been + participle. Yet keeps it in the present perfect.

quiz.prompt: The report _____ by the board. (sign off)
quiz.explain: The phrasal verb stays together and the doer goes behind by.
Last month is a finished time, so the past simple passive, not the present perfect.
I takes have been, and the participle of tell is told.
Has been suspended. Note that nobody is named as the suspender.
Happen has no object and therefore no passive.
Forms is plural, so have been, and send / sent / sent.
This year is unfinished, so the present perfect, and the police go without saying.
Have been moved says it happened to us. Have moved would say we did it.
Has been identified — and notice how completely the passive removes whoever made the error.

results: Clean run. You can turn a sentence around and you know when the doer is worth keeping.
Solid progress. Worth a look back at the active version before you go on.
Good first attempt. The auxiliary chain is the part to read again.
